messages.content:
You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Broadcom's ASIC Market Share Defense: Google TPU, MediaTek, and the 80% Mass Production Barrier

TEXT:
To prevent disconnection, feel free to follow our backup account, which will also share updates daily.
Google has handed part of the Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) supply chain to MediaTek, leading the market to speculate that Broadcom could see its market share reduced by half. Morgan Stanley’s counterargument focuses on three mass production requirements: high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, and large-scale system verification. Whether Broadcom can maintain around 80% revenue share will determine if its AI revenue estimate of $120 billion for FY2027 can be realized.
Breaking Down the Market Share Debate: Having a Second Supplier Doesn’t Equal Splitting Revenue Evenly
The market extrapolated MediaTek’s entry to mean Broadcom was being replaced. Google bringing on a second ASIC (Application Specific Integrated Circuit) partner is not unexpected. Google is highly cost-sensitive, wishes to reduce dependence on a single supplier, and is looking to purchase some generic components separately to reduce the markup paid to Broadcom. MediaTek has secured a credible opportunity in 3nm TPU, and there is a fact-based judgment within the supply chain regarding its entry into the project.
Divergence emerges when projecting market share. The pessimistic view is that once MediaTek passes the initial verification stage, Broadcom’s TPU share will quickly fall to 50% or even be completely replaced. Morgan Stanley’s baseline scenario is Broadcom maintains around 80% of TPU revenue in the long run, while MediaTek takes 15%—20%.
This proportion is also closer to both companies’ publicly stated long-term targets. Broadcom believes it can maintain more than 80% of the serviceable market, while MediaTek seeks a long-term ASIC market share around 20%.
Chip quantity can exaggerate the economic value that MediaTek will capture. MediaTek’s solution is priced significantly lower, so unit share does not equate directly to revenue share. Even using Morgan Stanley MediaTek team’s more optimistic shipment estimates, MediaTek’s revenue share next year would still be closer to 20%. If the market only looks at wafer numbers, foundry allocation, or initial orders, it’s easy to overestimate the impact on Broadcom’s revenue.
This debate is similar to previous discussions around Amazon Trainium’s supply chain. New suppliers can indeed secure meaningful projects, and original suppliers may lose part of their share; however, the market often prematurely reacts to “clients adding backup plans” as if “the incumbent supplier is being eliminated.” Morgan Stanley acknowledges MediaTek’s opportunity, but insists on seeing evidence of large-scale deliveries before downgrading Broadcom.
Broadcom’s Three Barriers to Mass Production: Memory, Packaging, and System Validation
The first barrier is high-bandwidth memory (HBM). One of MediaTek’s cost advantages is that Google can separately source some components rather than buying them as a package from Broadcom. But this calculation assumes critical parts can always be obtained at reasonable prices. HBM is currently in short supply, with spot prices already rising, and buying ad hoc may not be cheaper. Broadcom previously secured some supply contracts, and what once seemed routine procurement is now becoming an advantage in both cost and delivery.
HBM impacts more than just chip material costs. During shortages, only solutions with timely HBM supply are eligible for system integration and customer deployments. Even if MediaTek completes chip design, if it cannot secure enough competitively-priced HBM, it will be hard to deliver on Google’s overall cost reduction targets. Broadcom’s advantage therefore extends from design to supply assurance.
The second barrier is advanced packaging. Morgan Stanley anticipates MediaTek will be able to secure some wafer-level system integration packaging (CoWoS) capacity for 2nm TPU minimum production, but there is still uncertainty over whether Intel’s EMIB (Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge) can handle Google’s complexity. Substrate capacity could also become a bottleneck. The report sees EMIB as a solution that, if executed smoothly, could open up more scale and cost advantages around 2029, with CoWoS being a more reliable fallback.
This means 2nm projects shouldn’t calculate revenue based solely on the chip node. There are barriers between successful sampling, small batch risk production, and large-scale mass production—including packaging yield, substrates, memory, system validation, and delivery timeline. If any link is delayed, Google will prioritize the stability of its existing platforms, and Broadcom has already passed these hurdles.
[...]
The third barrier is large-scale system validation. TPUs need to operate continuously within large clusters; chipset performance is just a starting point. Suppliers must also pass system-level certification to assure stable coordination among multiple TPU racks and ensure that new solutions won’t disrupt Google’s AI infrastructure roadmap. A one-time tape out may bring initial revenue, but cannot prove thousands of chips, memory modules, networks, and software will be reliable at scale.
[...]
This is why Broadcom’s product sales include production certainty. Once customers set training and inference capacity on a timeline as part of capital expenditures, delays may cost more than the price difference for a single chip. While Google is eager to support an alternative supplier, it will avoid aggressive switching until the new solution proves its ability to scale.
[...]
Broadcom’s growth isn’t dependent on its Google TPU share remaining at 100%. Morgan Stanley forecasts Broadcom’s AI revenue to reach about $120 billion for fiscal 2027, tied to roughly 10GW of AI deployments.
[...]
Google’s internal and external TPU opportunities together account for about 75% of deployments. At about $10 billion—$12 billion in revenue per gigawatt, this corresponds to $80 billion in TPU-related revenue.
[...]
These figures provide a more practical analytical framework. Even if Broadcom cedes around 20% TPU revenue share, as long as Google’s overall deployment grows, absolute revenue can still increase. Investors need to look at both the total market and share—not merely cut Broadcom’s total AI revenue projection when MediaTek wins orders.
[...]
The key change for fiscal 2028 will be customer structure. Morgan Stanley expects Broadcom will then be able to support at least 15GW of AI deployment, with TPUs accounting for about 60% of AI revenue. That proportion will fall due to scaling up of other ASIC clients, not a weakening of Google’s business. Several new projects are expected to ramp up in the second half of 2027. Broadcom’s AI revenue will gradually shift from being driven by a single major customer to multi-client growth.
[...]
This shift will lessen the impact of Google market share debates on valuation. Before 2027, Google TPUs will remain the main pillar of Broadcom’s AI revenue; in FY 2028 and beyond, whether new clients can ramp up production on schedule will determine the revenue ceiling. If Broadcom maintains its position as Google’s primary supplier and brings new clients to scale, MediaTek capturing around 20% share may only be a controllable loss within an expanding market.
[...]
Morgan Stanley continues to rank Broadcom as the core AI computing pick after Nvidia. The report maintains an “overweight” rating and $502 target price, based on 28x expected 2027 calendar year EPS of $17.92. With a closing price of $384.05 prior to the report’s release, this implies about 31% potential upside.
